newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy budget seen shuffling funds, evading reforms.
newsitem.headline: Italy budget seen shuffling funds, evading reforms.

text.p: Italy's forthcoming mini-budget will strengthen its hand when founder members of the European single currency are picked, but will do nothing to tackle urgently needed spending reforms, analysts said on Thursday.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi promised earlier this year that the spring package of deficit-cutting measures would be based on structural savings, but with local elections looming and a key government ally in revolt, his options are limited.
"The mini-budget numbers might be fine, but the content is likely to be disappointing," said Francesco Giordano, economist with Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi has indicated that the package, due by the end of April, will raise around 14 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) in a final bid to reduce the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The deficit/GDP ratio hit 6.8 percent in 1996, and analysts are sceptical about Italy's chances of dragging it down to the three percent level required by the Maastricht Treaty framework for economic and monetary union (EMU).

"With the budget they have in mind, we won't get to three percent, but we will probably get close to what the Germans achieve and that will win Italy a negotiating position," said Lorenzo Codogno, head of research at Bank of America in Milan.
The elite group of states due to launch EMU in 1999 is due to be decided early next year.

Italy has made considerable strides in recent months in taming tearaway state expenditure but now has limited room for fresh savings. Economists say the most obvious areas of attack are the generous pensions system and inefficient health service.
But the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, has already warned it will block any reduction in welfare spending.
In addition, an assault on such sensitive areas would prove political dynamite ahead of the April 27 local elections in 1,138 Italian cities and towns, including Milan and Turin.
"I find it very hard to believe they will do anything structural like that two weeks before such important elections," said Giovanna Mossetti, head economist at Milan brokers Caboto.
So what can the government do?

Expected measures include transferring employee severance payment funds to Treasury coffers. Similar sleight of hand was pulled off by the French government last year, which added 37.5 billion francs ($6.6 billion) to accounts via a special transfer of pension funds from France Telecom.

Italy is expected to shunt up to eight trillion lire into the Treasury with such a move, despite opposition from Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, his small coalition party and from companies which use the funds as cash flow.

"It is a very appealing operation because macro-economically it is neutral. And even if it is a bit of an accounting trick, it can also be seen as structural, affecting future budgets," Giordano said.

The Treasury is also likely to introduce a one-off solidarity tax on the pensions of people who have taken early retirement in the past and there is talk that the Treasury might block people seeking early retirement this year.

With talk of possible pension reform filling the newspapers, unions say an astounding 100,000 workers have already filed for retirement in 1997 in a bid to beat any clampdown. Only 80,000 people retired in all of 1996.

While the bulk of the budget is likely to focus on these three areas, other action could include a further hike in some stamp duties, yet another tax amnesty and a lowering of government forecasts for debt servicing costs.
"There will be nothing to rejoice about in terms of structural changes...that is going to have to wait until the 1998 budget," Mossetti said. ($ = 1690 Italian Lire) ($ = 5.718 French Francs)
